nameStory: The Brown Pelican gets its straightforward name from its predominantly brown and gray plumage, which distinguishes it from its much larger cousin, the American White Pelican. Unlike many bird names that honor people or places, this one simply describes what you see - a large pelican that's mostly brown in color.
description: The Brown Pelican is a large, distinctive seabird with an enormous bill and expandable throat pouch that's unmistakable once you see it. These impressive birds have long, broad wings and webbed feet, with adults measuring about 4 feet long with a 6-7 foot wingspan. Their plumage changes dramatically between seasons - breeding adults sport striking white heads with yellowish crowns and dark maroon-brown necks, while non-breeding birds have white heads and necks year-round. They're famous for their spectacular fishing technique of diving headfirst into the water from heights up to 60 feet.

idTips.label: Massive Bill and Pouch
idTips.description: The enormous yellow-orange bill with its stretchy throat pouch is unmistakable - the pouch can hold up to 3 gallons of water and feels like wet leather when empty

idTips.label: Dramatic Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for spectacular headfirst dives from 20-60 feet up, creating a big splash as they plunge after fish - no other large bird in New England fishes this way

idTips.label: Seasonal Head Colors
idTips.description: Breeding adults have bright white heads with yellow crowns and rich maroon necks, while winter birds are white-headed all over with duller skin colors

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies in long lines or V-formations close to the water with slow, steady wingbeats alternating with glides - their wings make a distinctive whooshing sound

idTips.label: Large Webbed Feet
idTips.description: Huge grayish webbed feet that feel rough and leathery, perfectly designed for swimming and perching on posts and rocks

habitat: Brown Pelicans are rare visitors to New England's coastal waters, most often spotted along sandy beaches, rocky shores, harbors, and salt marshes from late spring through fall. They prefer areas with calm, shallow waters where fish are abundant, and you might see them resting on piers, jetties, or offshore rocks. Look for them around Cape Cod, the Islands, and other southern New England coastal areas where warmer waters attract the fish they depend on.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring visitors begin appearing in late April and May, usually single birds or small groups following fish migrations northward along the coast.
seasonality.summer: Peak sighting season when most observations occur, with birds in full breeding plumage showing off their striking white heads and maroon necks.
seasonality.fall: Occasional sightings continue through September and early October as birds move south, often in their duller non-breeding plumage.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter as these birds retreat to warmer southern waters where ice won't interfere with their diving fishing technique.

funFact: Brown Pelicans have built-in air bags throughout their bodies that act like bubble wrap, cushioning the impact when they slam into the water at 40+ mph during their spectacular fishing dives - without this natural protection, the impact would be fatal!
confusionNotes: In New England, Brown Pelicans are most likely confused with the much larger American White Pelican, but remember: Brown Pelicans dive for fish while White Pelicans never dive - they scoop fish from the surface. White Pelicans are also massive with bright white plumage and black wingtips, while Brown Pelicans are smaller and predominantly gray-brown.
contextualKnowledge: Brown Pelicans are considered rare vagrants in New England - they're really southern birds whose normal range extends only as far north as New Jersey. The 18 recorded sightings in New England represent wandering individuals, likely drawn north by warming ocean temperatures and abundant fish, making any sighting here a special treat for birdwatchers.
compareHints: Brown Pelicans are much smaller and more agile than their only relative in the region, the American White Pelican. While White Pelicans are enormous soaring birds with 9-foot wingspans that never dive, Brown Pelicans are built for spectacular plunge-diving with streamlined bodies and reinforced skulls. Brown Pelicans also have the distinctive gray-brown coloring year-round, while White Pelicans are brilliant white with black wingtips.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American White Pelicans are dramatically different from their Brown Pelican relatives – they're much larger, brilliant white instead of gray-brown, and have completely different feeding behaviors.
